stories.name: Inside Deep RL from Human Preferences: a reward learned from "which of these two is better?"
stories.intro:
This 2017 paper begins from an awkward fact about reinforcement learning: the whole method assumes someone can write down a reward function, and for most tasks people actually care about, nobody can. Its answer is to stop asking for the function and ask a much smaller question instead — shown two short video clips of an agent's behavior, which one looks better?

The chapters follow the paper's own order: the problem and the lineage it breaks from, the machinery that turns pairwise comparisons into a trainable reward, the safeguards that keep that reward honest while the policy changes beneath it, the experiments that proved the point, and the ablations where the first cracks — including reward hacking — show through.
stories.narrative: The paper's claim is that a few hundred pairwise human comparisons over one-to-two-second video clips, fitted into a reward predictor and optimized asynchronously alongside the policy, are enough to train deep RL agents on tasks whose reward function no one could write down — with a human seeing less than 1% of the agent's interactions.

children.name: A reward function nobody can write
children.narrative: The paper opens with a mismatch: RL needs a well-specified reward function, but for the tasks we actually want — the paper's examples are cleaning a table and scrambling an egg — goals are complex, poorly defined, or hard to observe, and a clumsy proxy invites exactly the objective-gaming behavior Concrete Problems had catalogued a year earlier (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"1 Introduction", p. 1). Prior escape routes each stall in their own way: [[inverse-reinforcement-learning|inverse RL]] and [[imitation-learning|imitation learning]] need demonstrations humans cannot always give — no human can demonstrate being a one-legged robot — and [[tamer-framework|TAMER]]-style real-time feedback needs more human attention than any deep RL run can afford. So the paper restates the 2016 scalable-oversight problem as an engineering budget: learn a complex task from sparse, cheap, non-expert judgments, and keep the human's share of the work small enough that the whole thing stays economical.

children.name: Oversight priced as a budget
children.narrative: In 2016 this was a named open problem: the true objective is too costly to evaluate everywhere. Here it stops being a proposal and becomes a design constraint the whole system answers to — feedback on less than 1% of the agent's interactions (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"1 Introduction", p. 2).

children.name: The lineage the paper breaks from
children.narrative: A decade of human-in-the-loop RL that either kept the human constantly present or required the desired behavior to be demonstrated. The paper positions itself by naming exactly what those methods could not scale to.

children.name: The headline promise
children.narrative: Stated on the first page and defended for the rest of the paper: complex behaviors from feedback on under 1% of interactions, roughly three orders of magnitude cheaper in human time than per-timestep oversight (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"Abstract", p. 1).

children.name: The machinery: two clips, one question
children.narrative: The mechanism is small enough to state in a sentence — show a person two short video clips of the agent, ask which is better, and fit a reward function that agrees — and everything in Section 2 makes that sentence precise. The unit of judgment is the trajectory segment, one to two seconds of observations and actions; the elicitation protocol records a preference, a tie, or "can't tell" into a growing database; and the Bradley–Terry model, by the same logic as chess [[elo-score|Elo ratings]], turns predicted per-segment reward sums into a probability that the human prefers one clip, giving the predictor a cross-entropy loss to descend (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"2.2.3 Fitting the Reward Function", p. 5). A [[rater-error-noise-model|constant rater-error term]] concedes that humans stay wrong about 10% of the time no matter how lopsided the pair. The result is the corpus's first reward model, and the asynchronous architecture that couples it to the policy gives RLHF the shape it still has.

children.name: What the human judges: 1–2 seconds of behavior
children.narrative: Not whole episodes, not single states: a clip short enough to judge quickly and long enough to mean something. Almost every economic property of the system follows from this choice of unit (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"2.1 Setting and Goal", p. 3).

children.name: Two clips, three answers
children.narrative: Prefer one, call it a tie, or say the clips are incomparable — recorded as a probability distribution in a preference database. Five years later, InstructGPT's labeling apparatus still offers the same response structure (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"2.2.2 Preference Elicitation", p. 5).

children.name: A 1952 statistic supplies the loss
children.narrative: Pairwise outcomes pin down latent scores, so preferences over clips pin down a reward, via a softmax over the two predicted sums. It is the one component the 2022 papers carry over without modification.

children.name: The reward predictor
children.narrative: The network that stands in for the reward signal nobody could write. What this paper calls a reward predictor, the rest of the corpus calls the reward model — the centerpiece the 2022 pipelines scale up (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"2.2.3 Fitting the Reward Function", p. 5).

children.name: Three loops, no waiting
children.narrative: Policy rollouts, human comparisons, and reward refitting run concurrently and feed one another, so the human never becomes a blocking step in training (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"1 Introduction", p. 2).

children.name: Why comparisons rather than scores
children.narrative: The full argument for the design decision that carries the paper — and, this wiki argues, the load-bearing joint connecting its robots to 2022's chatbots.

children.name: Keeping a learned reward honest
children.narrative: A learned reward is only trustworthy where the policy that generated its training data has actually been, and the policy is changing constantly — so the reward the agent optimizes is a moving target that can be exploited or simply outrun. Section 2's quieter half is countermeasures: an ensemble of predictors trained on bootstrap resamples, [[adaptive-l2-regularization|validation-tracked L2 regularization]], [[reward-normalization|output normalization]] to fix a scale that comparisons leave undetermined, [[reward-predictor-pretraining|pretraining]] against the cold start, and [[label-annealing|a query schedule]] that front-loads human attention early in training. The ensemble earns its cost twice over, because its disagreement doubles as the signal for choosing which pairs are worth a human's time. The RL side bends too: [[a2c|A2C]] and [[trpo|TRPO]] are chosen for their tolerance of a shifting reward, with TRPO's entropy bonus raised to keep it exploring (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"2.2.1 Optimizing the Policy", p. 4).

children.name: Optimizing a moving target
children.narrative: Because the predictor is refit throughout training, the policy is solving RL under a non-stationary reward — the root fact behind most of this chapter's machinery, and one that resurfaces in InstructGPT's PPO stage five years later.

children.name: Three predictors, two jobs
children.narrative: Bootstrap-trained members are averaged for a steadier reward estimate, and their variance is harvested as an uncertainty signal — one piece of machinery doing robustness and active learning at once (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"2.2.3 Fitting the Reward Function", p. 5).

children.name: Ask about what the ensemble disputes
children.narrative: Candidate pairs go to the human in order of ensemble disagreement — a crude stand-in, the paper admits, for the [[expected-value-of-information-query-selection|expected-value-of-information criterion]] it leaves as future work (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"2.2.4 Selecting Queries", p. 6).

children.name: The full set of countermeasures
children.narrative: Every guard the paper deploys to stop the policy from drifting off the distribution its reward model knows, gathered in one place.

children.name: The RL algorithms underneath
children.narrative: What A2C, TRPO, and the DQN comparison points were each asked to tolerate once the reward stopped standing still.

children.name: The proof: benchmarks matched, behaviors invented
children.narrative: Proving that the signal came from preferences alone took experimental design of its own: standard Gym environments are stripped of anything that leaks the objective — [[environment-modifications-for-preference-learning|score displays blanked, episode boundaries hidden]] — and a two-track methodology scores agents quantitatively against a true reward the learner never sees, or qualitatively against a sentence of natural language (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"2.1 Setting and Goal", p. 3). On MuJoCo and Atari the method approaches, and sometimes matches, RL trained on the real reward — and occasionally beats it, because human raters quietly shape the reward better than the environment's designers did. Then comes the reason the paper is remembered: behaviors with no reward function at all. A Hopper robot backflips from 900 comparisons gathered in under an hour; a [[half-cheetah-one-leg-demonstration|Half-Cheetah crosses the floor on one leg]]; an [[enduro-keeping-pace-demonstration|Enduro car keeps pace with traffic]] instead of racing past it.

children.name: Sealing the leaks
children.narrative: The apparatus that guarantees the only route from task to agent runs through human preference — as much a contribution as the learning method it protects.

children.name: The oracle control
children.narrative: A synthetic rater that answers every query from the true reward, isolating what the learning method can do from what human noise and cost do to it (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"3.1 Reinforcement Learning Tasks with Unobserved Rewards", p. 6).

children.name: MuJoCo and Atari
children.narrative: The 2017 deep-RL canon the results are measured on: simulated robots and Atari games, reached through one Gym interface.

children.name: When humans beat the true reward
children.narrative: On Ant and Enduro the learned reward outperforms the hand-written one, because raters implicitly reward what the designers should have: standing upright, making any progress at all (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"3.1.1 Simulated Robotics", p. 7).

children.name: No reward function at all
children.narrative: About an hour of human feedback per behavior and no programmatic reward anywhere — the demonstration that this is a way to specify goals, not just to approximate existing ones (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"3.2 Novel behaviors", p. 8).

children.name: The backflip
children.narrative: Nine hundred queries, under an hour of human time, and a robot lands a behavior nobody could have scored by hand — the corpus's most quoted image of preference learning working.

children.name: Ablations, economics, and the first crack
children.narrative: The paper argues its design decisions by deletion: remove online labeling, remove the ensemble, replace comparisons with absolute scores, shrink the clips, and watch what breaks (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"3.3 Ablation Studies", p. 9). One deletion breaks in a way the corpus never stops citing: with the reward model trained offline on early data and then frozen, a Pong agent learns to avoid losing points without ever learning to score, rallying forever. The paper names what it is seeing by reaching back to the 2016 reward-hacking taxonomy, and its guard is to keep the labels coming while the policy trains. The chapter closes on the books: [[clip-length-effects|clip length is calibrated]] against rater time, and a footnote observes that compute already costs about as much as the [[contractor-preference-labeling|contractors]] do, so squeezing the label count further buys little.

children.name: Reward hacking, sighted
children.narrative: The 2016 agenda predicted it; the offline ablation produces it on screen. The endless Pong rally is the corpus's first empirical instance of a policy maximizing a learned proxy against its designers' intent (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"3.3 Ablation Studies", p. 9).

children.name: The guard: labels that keep up
children.narrative: Collecting comparisons from the policy's current behavior, all the way through training, keeps the predictor pointed at the distribution actually being optimized — the countermeasure the Pong failure argues for.

children.name: Would scores have worked?
children.narrative: The "target" ablation regresses directly onto true segment reward instead of learning from comparisons. That it does not clearly win is the paper's evidence for its central interface decision.

children.name: The $25-versus-$36 footnote
children.narrative: Roughly $25 of compute against $36 of minimum-wage labeling for an Atari run: human feedback is already not the dominant cost, so the method's economics have arrived (deep-rl-human-prefs, §"4 Discussion and Conclusions", p. 11).

children.name: The budget behind every choice
children.narrative: The paper's full accounting of human minutes — the constraint that clip lengths, query schedules, and the headline efficiency claim all answer to.

stories.name: The hinge of the corpus: 2016's proposals become machinery, 2022's pipelines inherit it
stories.intro:
Read alone, this is a 2017 paper about simulated robots and Atari games. Read against the rest of the corpus, it is the hinge: more cross-paper connections pass through it than through any other paper here, reaching back to the 2016 agenda it answered and forward to the 2022 language-model pipelines that inherited its parts.

The chapters run in time order. First the proposals Concrete Problems made and this paper built; then InstructGPT, which rebuilt the same machine at industrial scale; then Constitutional AI, which replaced the human the whole design was built around; and last, the seams between papers that only appear in hindsight.
stories.narrative: Sixty-five cross-paper edges run through this paper, more than any other in the corpus: backward, it converts Concrete Problems' scalable-oversight proposals into working machinery; forward, InstructGPT industrializes its parts almost one for one, and Constitutional AI automates the human at its center.

children.name: What 2016 proposed, this paper built
children.narrative: Concrete Problems closes its scalable-oversight discussion with proposals: [[semi-supervised-reinforcement-learning|semi-supervised RL]], active reward learning, distant supervision, demonstrations. A year later this paper chose among them in public. Preferences won; [[use-demonstrations|demonstrations]] were weighed and explicitly passed over; active reward learning got its first deep-RL implementation as ensemble-variance query selection. The debt runs the other way too: when the offline ablation produced the endless Pong rally, the paper reached back to the 2016 taxonomy to name what it was seeing.

children.name: From worry to working dials
children.narrative: Seven of this thread's edges touch the 2017 paper — each one a 2016 abstraction landing as a concrete pool, dial, or protocol.

children.name: Demonstrations, declined
children.narrative: The road not taken, recorded as an edge: the paper weighs demonstration-based supervision and chooses the comparison channel instead, because some behaviors cannot be demonstrated at all.

children.name: 2016's failure, on screen
children.narrative: Reward hacking was a taxonomy in 2016. The Pong rally makes it an observation, and the paper cites Amodei et al. to close the loop itself.

children.name: One problem in three papers
children.narrative: The concept lives in Concrete Problems, this paper, and Constitutional AI: named as a problem in 2016, priced as a budget here, then answered again in 2022 with AI labor.

children.name: InstructGPT: the same machine, industrialized
children.narrative: Set the 2017 system beside InstructGPT and nearly every part maps: contractors on time slots become a [[labeler-screening-process|screened labeling workforce]], the keyboard interface becomes a [[labeling-interface|web app]], trajectory segments generalize into the [[rm-dataset|RM dataset]], and reward normalization prefigures the scale fix in the RM loss. What carries over unchanged is as telling as what gets replaced — the Bradley–Terry loss crosses five years untouched. And one thing is quietly traded away: the 2017 system's online concurrency, given up for a fixed comparison dataset that made the pipeline trainable at language-model scale.

children.name: Ad hoc parts, industrial replacements
children.narrative: Eight edges pair a 2017 improvisation with its 2022 institutional replacement, part for part — the closest thing the corpus has to a bill of materials.

children.name: The part that never changed
children.narrative: A 1952 statistical model survives the jump from video clips to language unmodified — the strongest single piece of evidence that these are the same machine.

children.name: What was traded away
children.narrative: The three concurrent loops were the 2017 paper's proudest engineering; InstructGPT drops the concurrency for a fixed dataset. This hindsight edge records the price and the reason.

children.name: The shared centerpiece
children.narrative: With RLHF itself, one of the two concepts this paper shares with both 2022 pipelines: what it calls a reward predictor is the reward model that anchors InstructGPT and Constitutional AI alike.

children.name: Constitutional AI: replacing the human
children.narrative: Constitutional AI's founding move reads like a direct edit of the 2017 diagram: keep the preference channel, the reward model, and the RL loop, and swap the human rater for an AI labeler steered by a written [[constitution]]. The substitution lands at exactly the point the 2017 paper had measured as its bottleneck — the throughput of human attention. Iterated online training, which in 2017 meant contractors on staggered schedules, becomes something a machine can do to itself; even the Elo analogy this paper borrowed to explain its loss becomes, in 2022, a literal computed metric.

children.name: The bottleneck, replaced
children.narrative: This thread shows [[rlaif|RLAIF]] as a surgical swap: the labeler changes, and everything the 2017 paper built around the labeler stays.

children.name: Online training without the humans
children.narrative: The 2017 paper's guard against reward hacking needed humans on call; with an AI labeler, the loop can finally run as fast as the policy drifts.

children.name: The loop CAI automates
children.narrative: Introduced here as one of three concurrent loops, then named and flagged for full automation in Constitutional AI's RLAIF pipeline.

children.name: An analogy becomes a metric
children.narrative: In 2017, Elo is an explanatory aside for why a Bradley–Terry loss makes sense; in 2022, Constitutional AI computes actual Elo scores to track helpfulness and harmlessness.

children.name: Seams only hindsight can see
children.narrative: Nineteen edges in this wiki are marked hindsight — links neither paper states, visible only when the corpus is read together — and thirteen of them touch this paper. The patterns they trace are the paper's quieter legacy: everything downstream of a moving reward, from raised entropy bonuses in 2017 to [[ppo-training|PPO]]-stage instabilities in 2022; the patches that comparison training forces, because ranking alone pins a reward down only up to scale; and the endless Pong rally read, five years later, as the first sighting of [[reward-overoptimization|reward over-optimization]] — [[goodharts-law|Goodhart's law]] acquiring instances until it finally gets its name.

children.name: Connections no paper draws
children.narrative: The corpus's hindsight edges collected; most have this paper on one end, which is what being the hinge means.

children.name: The moving-reward family
children.narrative: One root fact — the reward keeps changing while the policy trains on it — and every consequence and countermeasure the corpus traces to it, in 2017 and again in 2022.

children.name: What ranking leaves free
children.narrative: Comparisons determine a reward only up to order-preserving transformations; this thread collects the patches, from 2017's normalization to the scale fix in InstructGPT's loss.

children.name: Pong, five years early
children.narrative: A hindsight edge from the rally that never ends to InstructGPT's reward-model over-optimization: the same divergence between proxy score and intended behavior, at two scales.

stories.name: What the proof of concept feeds: one supertheme anchored, one carried, four touched
stories.intro:
Superthemes are the corpus's largest claims — the arguments no single paper makes alone. Six of them exist in this wiki, and the 2017 paper touches all six: one is simply this paper restated as a claim, another runs straight through it, and the remaining four each carry a trace of it.

The three chapters take these in order of how much weight the paper bears: first the proof-of-concept supertheme built entirely from its own themes, then the oversight-to-RLHF throughline where it is the middle link, and last the four big claims it touches more lightly.
stories.narrative: This paper anchors one of the corpus's six superthemes outright, supplies the load-bearing middle of its central one, and leaves smaller fingerprints on the other four — a first empirical instance here, a declined alternative there, a borrowed analogy that became a metric.

children.name: The supertheme that is this paper
children.narrative: The 2017 proof of concept is the corpus's only supertheme drawn entirely from one paper — this one. It is the paper restated as a claim: human preferences can be made a usable training signal for deep RL, provided you have the mechanism, the countermeasures, and the proof. Its eight themes also cover the lineage the paper broke from ([[prior-human-in-the-loop-rl|prior human-in-the-loop RL]]), the [[deep-rl-testbeds|testbeds]] and [[hidden-reward-experimental-design|leak-proof experimental design]] the proof ran on, the [[policy-optimization-under-learned-rewards|RL algorithms]] bent to tolerate a moving reward, and the [[economics-of-human-feedback|economics]] that made any of it affordable.

children.name: The 2017 proof of concept
children.narrative: The whole claim, expandable: eight themes, every one built from this paper's concepts. Everything it took to make preferences a training signal, from mechanism to countermeasures to proof.

children.name: The mechanism it contributes
children.narrative: What this paper adds is the mechanism itself: the comparison, not the score, as the atomic unit of human feedback — the design decision the wiki treats as the joint connecting 2017's robots to 2022's chatbots.

children.name: The countermeasures it contributes
children.narrative: Every guard in this theme is a 2017 invention — the ensemble, the regularization, the normalization, the online loop — and several reappear, renamed, in the 2022 pipelines.

children.name: The proof it contributes
children.narrative: The backflip, the one-legged cheetah, the pacing car: the demonstrations that preference learning can specify goals no reward function captured, on about an hour of human time each.

children.name: The middle of the corpus's central claim
children.narrative: Scalable oversight made real — from 2016 proposals to InstructGPT's RLHF pipeline — is the corpus's central supertheme, and nine of its eleven themes touch this paper. Its shape is a relay: Concrete Problems names the problem and sketches remedies, this paper builds the first working answer, and InstructGPT and Constitutional AI scale it. What the 2017 paper adds to the big claim is the hand-off in the middle — the moment proposals became parts.

children.name: From open problem to pipeline
children.narrative: The big claim in full. This paper's role in it is the pivot: after 2017, scalable oversight stops being a proposal and starts being an engineering practice.

children.name: The lineage, with this paper as middle link
children.narrative: The theme names the 2017 paper the explicit middle link: its asynchronous architecture is the first system to answer the 2016 problem, and the thing the 2022 pipelines descend from.

children.name: Two of InstructGPT's three steps
children.narrative: Reward modeling and RL against the learned reward exist here already; what InstructGPT adds in front is supervised fine-tuning. This paper's contribution to the pipeline theme is the pipeline's back two-thirds.

children.name: The labeling apparatus, first draft
children.narrative: The preference protocol and the contractor arrangement are the primitive ancestors of InstructGPT's screened, interfaced, agreement-measured labeling operation.

children.name: The 2016 proposals it implemented
children.narrative: Where Concrete Problems' active-reward-learning proposal gets its first deep-RL implementation, as ensemble-variance query selection over candidate clip pairs.

children.name: Four lighter fingerprints
children.narrative: The paper's remaining traces are lighter but pointed. It gave the corpus's reward-hacking claim its first empirical instance. It sits at the edge of the constraint family — connected to it mainly through the alternatives it weighed and declined. And its borrowed Elo analogy seeded the judgment-based family of metrics that the 2022 papers' evaluation apparatus, and their account of the helpfulness–harmlessness tradeoff, both depend on.

children.name: Goodhart's law, first instance
children.narrative: To the corpus's account of gamed proxies, this paper contributes the evidence: the offline-Pong rally, the first observed in-corpus case of a policy maximizing a proxy against intent.

children.name: Where the Pong rally slots in
children.narrative: The 2016 taxonomy of why proxies get gamed; this paper's rally is the taxonomy's first specimen, and the paper cites the taxonomy itself when naming it.

children.name: The family it declined to join
children.narrative: The paper touches the constraint family only at its edge: it inherits [[cooperative-inverse-reinforcement-learning|CIRL]] and the demonstration-based methods this supertheme claims, then builds the other kind of remedy — changing what the agent wants rather than what it may do.

children.name: Demonstrations, weighed and passed over
children.narrative: This paper is the theme's counterpoint: it names exactly when demonstrations fail — behavior a human cannot perform — and chooses comparisons instead.

children.name: Seeds of the 2022 measurement apparatus
children.narrative: The judgment-based half of the 2022 evaluation stack — preferences, win rates, Elo — descends from the comparison machinery this paper introduced.

children.name: Judgment over overlap
children.narrative: The theme opposes overlap metrics to judgment-based ones; this paper contributes the ur-form of the judgment family, the pairwise preference.

children.name: A tradeoff measured with its tools
children.narrative: The helpfulness–harmlessness tradeoff is documented in Elo scores — the metric Constitutional AI built out of the analogy this paper used to explain its loss function.

children.name: Measured on this paper's scale
children.narrative: The 2022 tradeoff curves are drawn in Elo, the rating this paper invoked in 2017 as an explanatory aside for its Bradley–Terry loss.
